reading.isBillReading: A stage in passing a law
reading.explain_preliminary: Preliminary reading — the first stage of a private bill. If it passes, the bill goes to committee to prepare it for the first reading.
reading.explain_first: First reading — the plenum approves the bill's principles and sends it to committee for detailed work.
reading.explain_second: Second reading — a vote on each clause and on reservations, after the committee has prepared the bill.
reading.explain_third: Third reading — the final vote; if it passes, the bill becomes law.
reading.explain_second_third: Second & third reading — the bill's final approval.
reading.explain_agenda: Motion for the agenda — a request to hold a plenum debate on a public issue. It is not a bill and has no readings.
reading.explain_noConfidence: A motion of no confidence in the government.
reading.explain_reservation: A vote on a reservation — an objection to a clause of a bill during the second reading.
reading.explain_secondaryLegislation: Approval of secondary legislation (regulations or orders) made by the executive.
reading.explain_continuity: Continuity — continuing the legislative process of a bill from a previous Knesset.
reading.explain_committeeReferral: Referring the bill to a committee for discussion.
reading.explain_decision: Approval of a Knesset motion, decision, or announcement.

statement.title: Accessibility Statement
statement.intro: "Our Knesset" strives to provide a convenient and equal experience for all users, including people with disabilities, and works to make its content accessible in the spirit of equality and human dignity.
statement.conformance: The site's level of accessibility: Israeli Standard IS 5568, level AA (the standard is based on WCAG 2.0, level AA). We build and check the site against WCAG 2.2, level AA.
statement.testing: We check the site with automated AccessLint scans and by using it with a keyboard only.
statement.features: Every page has an accessibility button at the bottom of the screen. It opens a menu with these options:
statement.featuresSaved: Your choices are saved only in your browser, on your device. Details in the <link>cookie policy</link>.
statement.limitations: Some text that comes from the Knesset appears only in Hebrew until it is translated. Charts have a text alternative where possible.
statement.contact: Ran into an accessibility problem? Tell us:
statement.fix: We will fix problems reported to us within 60 days.

privacy.title: Privacy policy
privacy.intro: In short: the site keeps no data about you, uses no cookies and does not track you. Here is exactly what happens when you use it.
privacy.keepTitle: What the site keeps about you
privacy.keep: Nothing. The site keeps no data about its visitors.
privacy.logs: The site is hosted by Vercel. Vercel keeps standard server logs, which include IP addresses. We will set the shortest retention period for them.
privacy.cookies: The site uses no cookies. The language you choose is kept in the page address, not in a cookie.
privacy.storage: Your browser stores only two things, and only if you choose them. They are kept in localStorage, on your own device:
privacy.storageA11y: a11y-settings — your choices in the accessibility menu.
privacy.clear: To delete them: the "Reset settings" button in the accessibility menu deletes the accessibility settings, and you can delete both in your browser's settings (by clearing the site's data).
privacy.tracking: The site has no analytics, no trackers, no ads, no scripts from other sites and no embedded players or widgets. So a "Do Not Track" or GPC signal is respected by design: there is nothing to turn off.
privacy.othersTitle: What your browser loads from others
privacy.othersWikimedia: Photos of members and party logos load from upload.wikimedia.org, so your browser contacts Wikimedia to show them.
privacy.othersGithub: The buttons for reporting a mistake or suggesting information open a ticket form on GitHub (github.com) with what you wrote. A ticket is opened only if you submit the form there. On GitHub, <link>GitHub's privacy policy</link> applies.
privacy.othersSearch: What you type in search stays on the site's server. It is not sent to any third party.
privacy.compass: The <link>election compass</link> runs only in your browser. Your answers are not saved and not sent anywhere. The same will be true of the "find parties" tool, coming soon.
privacy.recordsTitle: The public records we publish, and your rights
privacy.records: The site publishes public records about Knesset members, candidates and lobbyists. They come from public sources: the Knesset's open data, the Central Elections Committee, Wikidata and Wikimedia Commons.
privacy.rights: Under the Protection of Privacy Law, 1981, if the site has information about you, you have the right to see it (section 13) and to ask for it to be corrected (section 14). To make a request, contact us as shown below.
privacy.contact: Questions about privacy, or a request to see or correct information:

terms.title: Terms of use
terms.intro: In short: this is an unofficial information site about the Knesset. Every fact has a source, but mistakes are possible, so check important details at the source.
terms.unofficial: "Our Knesset" is an unofficial site. It is not affiliated with the Knesset or the Central Elections Committee.
terms.info: The site is for information only. We provide the information as is, with no warranty that it is complete, accurate or up to date. It may contain mistakes. Before you rely on an important detail, check it at the source.
terms.corrections: Found a mistake? Press "Report incorrect information" on the page where it appears, or open a ticket on the <link>tickets page</link>.
terms.correctionsHow: Nothing on the site changes automatically. We review every request, and correct the site when a source shows a mistake. Information about people is published only when a reliable source backs it.
terms.sources: Every fact on the site comes with its source, so you can check it yourself. All our sources are listed on the <link>data sources page</link>.
terms.compassTitle: The compass is not voting advice
terms.compass: The <link>election compass</link> shows how close your answers are to the lists' documented positions. It does not tell you whom to vote for — that choice is yours.
terms.licensesCode: The site's code: the <license>GNU AGPL</license> license, version 3 or any later version. <link>The code on GitHub</link>.
terms.licensesText: The texts we wrote for the site: <link>CC BY-SA 4.0</link> — you may reuse them if you credit the source and share them under the same license.
terms.licensesData: Data and photos: each under its own license. See <sources>data sources</sources> and <credits>credits</credits>.
terms.endorse: The site does not endorse or recommend any party, list or candidate.
terms.law: Israeli law applies to the use of the site and to these terms.

quiz.title: Election compass — who is closest to your views?
quiz.subtitle: Statements about what the lists want — security, religion and state, the economy, society and institutions. Every list has a documented stance — a Knesset vote, a platform or a statement — or "no stated position".
quiz.intro: Mark how much you agree with each statement (you can skip). After at least {min} answers you will see which lists are closest to your views, and why. The lists’ stances come from a documented source for every cell — a roll-call vote in the Knesset, the platform the list published, or the words of its leader as reported by a major outlet — never from the site’s interpretation. A list with no documented stance on a statement is simply not compared on it. Nothing is stored or sent anywhere.
quiz.positionsLink: See every stance with its source
quiz.disclaimer: The match is computed from closeness of positions only and is not a recommendation on how to vote.
quiz.sourcesNote: Every stance links to its source: the Knesset’s vote record, the platform, or the article.
quiz.important: This matters to me most (double weight)
quiz.resultsTitle: The lists closest to your views
quiz.resultsHow: The percentage = how close the list’s stances are to your answers, on average over the {n} statements you answered (only where the list has a documented stance).
quiz.thinCoverage: few documented stances — take with caution
quiz.voteRule: How a Knesset vote becomes a number: when almost all of a faction voted the same way (nine in ten or more) — "strongly"; when the faction split — "agree" or "disagree"; if fewer than half the faction voted, the stance is shown weaker and says so. A vote by a predecessor faction (e.g. Yesh Atid for Together) is marked explicitly.
quiz.topicsNote: What is here and what is not: 16 statements — security and foreign policy, the economy, religion and state, society and institutions. A statement enters the compass only if most lists (at least 8 of 15) have a documented stance on it. A statement on state intervention in housing and prices was left out for that reason — most platforms talk about competition and say nothing about supervision or public building, which is not a stance.
quiz.noStanceAtAll: no documented stance on any statement you answered — not compared
quiz.noStanceOn: The list has no documented stance on
quiz.explainScore: For each list we measured how close your answers are to its documented stances, statement by statement, and averaged. 100% = exactly the same stance on every statement; 0% = the opposite end on every statement.
quiz.explainImportant: A statement you marked as especially important counts double.
quiz.explainNoStance: A statement on which a list has no documented stance is not counted for it — neither for nor against. That is why each list shows how many statements it was compared on.
quiz.explainSources: Every list stance links to its source — a Knesset vote, a platform or a quote — under "Why?".
quiz.explainNotAdvice: This is closeness of positions only, not a voting recommendation: the compass does not measure leadership, credibility or the past.
quiz.explainThin: A list compared on only a few statements can score very high or very low by chance; it is shown dimmed and ranked after the lists compared on most of your statements.

lobbyists.title: Lobbyists
lobbyists.subtitle: Who lobbies the Knesset, for which firm, and on behalf of which clients.
lobbyists.explainer: A lobbyist is a person paid to advance the interests of clients — companies, organizations or groups — with MKs and committees. By law, lobbyists must register with the Knesset and disclose their clients. The list below is based on the Knesset's official lobbyist registry.
lobbyists.searchPlaceholder: Search a lobbyist, firm or client…
lobbyists.foreignBody: Beyond lobbying, foreign influence can also flow through money: donations from foreign political entities (foreign states or public bodies) to Israeli NGOs and organizations. The law requires organizations to report such donations — who gave, how much, and for what purpose — so the public can see who funds political or public activity.
lobbyists.foreignNote: Per-donation data is published by the Registrar of Non-Profits and on GuideStar and is not available here as structured open data.
lobbyists.whatForNote: What they were paid for and why: the registry lists each lobbyist's clients — the interest groups paying them to advance their positions in the Knesset — and the representation type (permanent or temporary). The client's identity indicates the interest being promoted; the registry does not list the specific bills or topics.
lobbyists.namesTransliterated: Lobbyists' names are transliterated by this site; the official spelling is the Hebrew one in the Knesset's lobbyist registry.

polls.title: Seat polls
polls.intro: Polls are a snapshot, not a forecast. Every number here was taken from the original article of the outlet that published it (or its publishing group’s report) and links to it. {count} polls from {institutes} polling institutes, {from}–{to}.
polls.blackoutText: Under the Elections (Propaganda Methods) Law, from the end of the Friday before election day until the polls close, no new election-poll results may be published. The polls here were published earlier: they are not current, and they cannot tell you how people will vote or what the public thinks today.
polls.averageMethod: The average of the {n} latest polls — one per polling institute ({from}–{to}). How it is computed — in the explanation below.
polls.threshold: electoral threshold — 3.25% of the votes (≈4 seats)
polls.trendHint: Choose a list to see how many seats each poll gave it since the lists closed.
polls.trendAria: Line chart: seats for each list in every poll, by date
polls.allCaption: List columns are in a fixed order (the site’s registry order), not by results; on phones each poll is shown in its own seat order. "<" — reported below the threshold; "—" — not reported.
polls.blocsTitle: The bloc map, as each outlet counted it
polls.blocsNote: Bloc membership is the pollster’s assumption, not the site’s: which list belongs to which bloc is decided differently in each poll. The figures are shown exactly as published.
polls.methodologySample: Sample and margin of error: a poll of about 500 respondents carries a sampling error of about 4 percentage points — a seat or two for a large list. A one-seat difference between polls is usually noise, not a trend.
polls.methodologyHouses: Why institutes differ: internet panels versus telephone, weighting by past vote, how undecided and unlikely voters are handled — all of these are systematic and produce steady gaps between houses. That is why the average takes one poll per institute.
polls.methodologyAverage: The average: each institute’s latest poll from the last {window} days, with equal weight, no smoothing and no quality weighting. A list a poll reported below the threshold counts as 0 seats in that poll. The range beside each list shows how far the houses disagree.
polls.methodologyScope: What is included: every seat poll published from {cutoff} — the day the candidate lists closed — onward, from every outlet we found. Earlier polls measured lists that no longer exist. No poll was left out because of its results.
polls.methodologyVerification: Verification: every figure was entered from the publishing outlet’s own article (or its own infographic), never from an aggregator, and the totals were checked against 120. Found an error? Tell us.
polls.notEnteredTitle: Polls we know of that were not entered
polls.homeMethod: Mean of {polls} polls from {institutes} institutes since the lists closed · {from}–{to}
polls.homeCta: Every poll, the blocs and the method
polls.indexCredit: The poll indexes we relied on so that no poll is left out
polls.perPollCredit: Every row: the outlet that published and the institute that conducted, linked to the original article.
polls.averageBelow: in {m} of {n} polls it does not enter the Knesset
polls.trendHouseNote: Each dot is one poll (hover to see who ran it and when). A thin line joins polls by the same institute — so a steady gap between lines is a difference in polling method, not a real change.
polls.belowAll: below the threshold in all {n} polls

positions.title: What the lists say — stance by stance
positions.subtitle: Every list against every statement in the election compass. Each cell is a documented stance — a Knesset vote, a platform or a statement — linked to its source. "—" means we found no stated position, not that the list is neutral.
positions.legend: Filled blue — agrees with the statement, outlined — disagrees, grey — neither. Click a cell to open the source.
positions.matrixPhone: The full table shows on wide screens; on a narrow screen choose a list above.
positions.method: Stances were taken from roll-call votes in the Knesset (the Knesset’s record), from the platforms the lists published, and from the words of list leaders as reported by major outlets; no stance was inferred from ideology. A vote becomes "strongly" only when almost the whole faction voted one way; when fewer than half the faction voted, the strength is capped and the cell says so. A vote by a predecessor faction is marked explicitly.
